mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about multiple (double or triple) covalent bonds is a common misconception?

options.A: A double bond consists of one sigma (σ) bond and one pi (π) bond.
options.B: Multiple bonds are always stronger than single bonds between the same two atoms.
options.C: Pi bonds are formed by the sideways overlap of p orbitals.
options.D: Sigma bonds allow free rotation of bonded atoms around the bond axis.

mcqs.answer: Multiple bonds are always stronger than single bonds between the same two atoms.
mcqs.explanation: Option B is the misconception. While double and triple bonds are generally stronger than a single bond between the same atoms, the increase in bond strength is not simply additive because pi bonds are weaker than sigma bonds and are more susceptible to breaking. Therefore, it is incorrect to claim that multiple bonds are always stronger in every context. Option A correctly describes the composition of a double bond. Option C correctly explains pi bond formation. Option D correctly states that sigma bonds permit free rotation, whereas pi bonds restrict rotation.

mcqs.question: Which of the following Lewis structures correctly represents the molecule carbon dioxide (CO₂)?

options.A: O=C=O with each O atom having two lone pairs and carbon having no lone pairs.
options.B: O–C–O with each O atom having three lone pairs and carbon having one lone pair.
options.C: O≡C≡O with each O atom having one lone pair and carbon having no lone pairs.
options.D: O=C–O with each O atom having two lone pairs and carbon having one lone pair.

mcqs.answer: O=C=O with each O atom having two lone pairs and carbon having no lone pairs.
mcqs.explanation: Option A shows the correct Lewis structure for CO₂: carbon forms two double bonds (each consisting of one sigma and one pi bond) with the two oxygen atoms, satisfying the octet rule for all atoms. Each oxygen has two lone pairs, and carbon has no lone pairs. Option B depicts single bonds only, which would leave carbon with an incomplete octet. Option C shows triple bonds, which would give carbon 10 electrons, violating the octet rule. Option D shows a single and a double bond, again leaving carbon with an incomplete octet.

mcqs.question: Two resonance structures of the nitrate ion (NO₃⁻) are shown below. In Structure I, nitrogen is double‑bonded to one oxygen and single‑bonded to the other two oxygens (each bearing a negative charge). In Structure II, nitrogen is double‑bonded to a different oxygen, with the same pattern of charges. Which structure has the lower total sum of absolute formal charges on all atoms?

options.C: Both structures have the same total sum of absolute formal charges
options.D: Neither structure satisfies the octet rule, so formal charge cannot be compared

mcqs.answer: Both structures have the same total sum of absolute formal charges
mcqs.explanation: Both resonance structures of NO₃⁻ are equivalent; the formal charges are: nitrogen +1, the double‑bonded oxygen 0, each single‑bonded oxygen –1. The absolute values sum to |+1| + |0| + |‑1| + |‑1| = 3 for each structure. Hence, the total sum of absolute formal charges is identical, making option C correct. Options A and B incorrectly assume one resonance form is better. Option D is wrong because both structures satisfy the octet rule and formal charges can be compared.

mcqs.question: In the formation of the ammonium ion (NH₄⁺), which of the following bonds is a coordinate (dative) covalent bond?

options.A: The bond between nitrogen and the hydrogen atom that was originally part of NH₃.
options.B: The bond formed when the lone pair on nitrogen is donated to a proton (H⁺).
options.C: All four N–H bonds in NH₄⁺ are identical covalent bonds formed by sharing electrons equally.
options.D: The bond between two hydrogen atoms in the ion.

mcqs.answer: The bond formed when the lone pair on nitrogen is donated to a proton (H⁺).
mcqs.explanation: Option B correctly identifies the coordinate covalent bond: nitrogen donates its lone pair to an incoming proton (H⁺), creating a N–H bond where both electrons originate from nitrogen. Option A describes a regular covalent bond formed by sharing electrons from both atoms. Option C is partially true after formation, but only one of the four N–H bonds is initially a coordinate bond; the others are ordinary covalent bonds. Option D is irrelevant because there is no H–H bond in NH₄⁺. Recognizing coordinate bonds is essential for understanding polyatomic ion formation, a common competitive‑exam topic.
